spans.text: The Kos-Pothia ferry held the late-afternoon Aegean light on its deck at four-fifteen on Tuesday the eighteenth of August 2026.

Tia Theodorakis-Coffin stood at the rail at the port-side, her two duffels at her feet. The wind off the channel pushed her hair back from her face. Eighteen years and eleven months old. Five-leg journey closing. Perth to Singapore Sunday. Singapore to Athens Monday. Athens to Kos Tuesday morning. Kos to Pothia by ferry Tuesday afternoon, the fifth and last leg, an hour and forty minutes from the Mastichari port.
She held her hands at the rail.

The Aegean late-summer water held its pale-blue. The Pothia coast rose ahead. The old town climbed the hill in white and ochre. The cathedral bell-tower stood at the centre, the kastro on a ridge above. The harbour mouth opened. Two fishing-cooperative boats were already at the wharves.
Pothia.
The ferry slowed coming through the breakwater at four-forty. Tia picked up the duffels and walked down to the lower deck.

The Pothia-port gate at four-fifty held the late-afternoon shadow at the limestone wall. Tia set the two duffels at the pavement. The five-o’clock Kos-Pothia ferry was already pulling away from the pier. Late-summer Aegean air carried the salt and the diesel smell across the gate. A woman in a pale-blue apron sat at a step at the side of the harbour road with a tin cup of coffee.

The Pothia harbour held the late-afternoon light on the east-facing water. The pre-twentieth-century stone and stucco of the old town climbed the hill in white and ochre. Fishing boats and cooperative boats moved at the wharves.
She held her hands at her lap.

Phaedon had arrived two days earlier, Sunday the sixteenth, first of the five. The other three, Niko and Lina and Athena, were coming this week or next. The five-lead cohort would be full by the end of August.
She picked up the duffels.
She walked from the port gate uphill toward the old town and the Pothia-Drosos-house.

The harbour road climbed slowly. Past the ticket office. Past the tackle shop. Past the cafe where two men sat with small white coffees and a third man stood at the counter. The men looked at her without comment. She walked on.
At the first cross-lane she turned uphill.

The lane went steeper and shadier between two-story whitewashed houses with iron balconies and shutters in two colours of blue. A washing line ran across the lane above her at the second-floor level, three white sheets and a child’s pale-yellow dress. A cat watched her from a step. A scooter went past on a cross-street below and the noise bounced off the walls and went away in a second.
She walked the duffels up.

The second cross-lane she took the right turn. Two-story stone, the limestone the same age as the kastro. The cathedral bell-tower rose between the houses on her left. A woman stood at a doorway with a small broom and looked at her.
The woman said: kalisperá.
Tia said: kalisperá.

The third lane was wider, blue-shaded by an awning across two buildings. She stopped at a whitewashed door with a small brass plate beside it. The plate had nothing on it. It had been polished where the screws were.
She set the duffels at the step.
She held her hands at her lap for the count of three.
She lifted the iron knocker. She knocked twice.
The Drosos house stood three blocks up from the port, in the upper old-town block. The family had lived in the house since 1903. The Pothia cooperative kept it now as the five-lead cohort dorm.
The door opened to Yiayia Marigoula, the current resident, seventy-six in 2026.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Tia.
Tia said: Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the Tuesday-eighteenth-five-twenty Tia-arrival.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: come in.
Tia came in. She set the duffels at the entry and took off her shoes. She put on the house slippers Yiayia Marigoula had set out for the cohort, five pairs, one for each lead, pre-arrival.

The entrance hall was tiled in a black-and-white pattern. The wall on her left had a row of iron hooks. A jacket she did not recognize hung at the second hook. The wall on her right had a small framed photograph she did not look at. The corridor ran back to a doorway with bright light beyond it.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the west bedroom is yours. Second floor.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Phaedon arrived Sunday.
Tia said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: east bedroom. He is at the front-room piano now.

Tia listened. The piano was on Bach Prelude No. 1 in C major, BWV 846, slow. The notes carried through the corridor without rush. One bar at a time. The sustaining pedal held the harmonic across the bar-line.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the evening piano-pattern. He has held it since Sunday.
Tia said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Phaedon came in at the four-o’clock ferry on the sixteenth. First of the five.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Aurelia-Drosos-Trakas line. Athens-Nea-Smyrni. Yiayia-Areti at Athens. The Drosos-line through his mother.
Tia said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the cohort line crosses at this house. Year 1.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: up you go.
Tia carried the duffels up the staircase.

The staircase was stone for the first flight, wood for the second. The wall held three framed photographs she did not stop to look at. The light from the second-floor landing fell at the top of the staircase in a wedge.

The second floor held five bedrooms for the five-lead cohort: north-east for Athena, north for Niko, north-west for Lina, west for Tia, east for Phaedon. Each door had a small wooden plaque with the name burned into the grain. The plaques had been set Saturday by Stelios.
She walked to the west bedroom.

The room held a single bed at the south wall, a wooden desk at the east wall, a wooden chair at the desk, a bedside table at the bed, a wardrobe at the west wall, and a west-facing window onto the old-town roofs uphill. The bedding was white. The wardrobe was empty. The desk was empty. The window was open at three inches.
She set the duffels at the bed and sat.
She held her hands at her lap.

She held five pictures at the back of her head as a single shape: the Perth-Singapore-Athens-Kos-Pothia five-leg journey from Sunday the sixteenth to Tuesday the eighteenth; the Broome-Theodorakis-Coffin family house at Carnarvon Street and her parents and Marisol her older sister at the Perth-airport farewell on Sunday (Marisol twenty-five, in for the day from Perth); her Anglo-Australian grandmother, Marisol Reyes-Coffin, born Perth 1956, who had given a Sunday blessing at the house; her Kalymnian-Australian grandfather, Stathis Theodorakis, born Broome 1947, second-generation, who had given a Sunday blessing also.

The Sunday-blessings at the family-house ran the Saturday-evening-pre-flight pattern. Marisol Reyes-Coffin at the kitchen at six in the evening with the small Greek-Orthodox-blessing-card. Stathis Theodorakis at the side at the second-small-card. Tia’s father’s mother Vera at the third-card-private at the back-of-the-chair-register, the card folded in half and her name in her own hand at the corner.

The Sunday-morning-flight at Broome-International-Airport at ten in the morning. Christos at the wheel of the ute. Susan at the side. Marisol at the back. The duffel-side-pocket held the three-blessing-cards.

The five-leg journey ran the Broome-Perth at eleven Sunday-morning Broome. Perth-Singapore at two-thirty Sunday-afternoon. The Singapore-overnight at the airport-hotel-room. Singapore-Athens at six in the morning Monday Singapore. Athens-Kos at three Monday-afternoon Athens. Kos-Mastichari at six Monday-evening Athens-time / four Monday-evening Kos-time. The Mastichari-Pothia-ferry at four-twenty Tuesday-afternoon Pothia-time.
Forty-eight hours of travel from Broome to Pothia.

A sixth picture stayed at the back of the chair. Yiayia Vera at the kitchen-doorway on Saturday evening with the folded blessing-card in her hand. Eighty in 2026. Born Broome 1946. Her father’s mother, the Yawuru-line grandmother. The greeting that ran private. Tia would keep that one at Pothia.
The shape held the late-afternoon Tuesday-eighteenth Pothia-Drosos-house-west-bedroom arrival.

She got up at five-thirty-five and walked to the window. The old-town roofs ran uphill in late-afternoon light. The cathedral-bell-tower rose to her left at three blocks. She set her hands at the sill. The window-frame was painted a flat blue, the paint chipped at the bottom-corner.
She thought one sentence at the back of the chair:
Pothia.
She walked back to the bed and started to unpack.
She opened the first duffel.

She set the four white shirts at the wardrobe rod on hangers. She set the three pairs of grey trousers at the rod. She set the two navy cardigans on hangers. She set the two skirts at the rod. She set the underclothes at the wardrobe drawer. She set the socks at the second drawer.

She set the Moleskine Year-1 archive-notebook at the wooden desk. The Moleskine was the family’s standard issue, a black 240-page lined notebook with a quarter-leather corner. She set the pen at the side of the Moleskine. She set the second pen at the back.

She set the Broome-Theodorakis-Coffin family photograph at the bedside table. The photograph showed her father, mother, Marisol, Tia at Cable Beach in July 2026 before her departure. The Indian Ocean was at the back. Marisol was at the right with her arm at Tia’s shoulder. Her father stood at the left with his hand at her mother’s back.

She set her grandmother Marisol’s Sunday-blessing card at the bedside table next to the photograph. The card was cream-coloured, the handwriting in dark-blue ink. Tia-mou. From your Yiayia Marisol, Broome, Sunday the sixteenth of August 2026. The Reyes-Coffin line carries.

She set her grandfather Stathis’s Sunday-blessing card next to that one. The card was the same cream colour. The handwriting was firmer. Tia-mou. From your Pappous, Broome, Sunday the sixteenth of August 2026. The Theodorakis line carries. Pothia, Broome, both directions.
The third card, the one from her father’s mother, she put inside the Moleskine front cover, closed. Year 1 private. Back of the chair.
She finished the first duffel at six-thirty.

She opened the second duffel for two minutes to set the second-pair of shoes at the floor under the bed and the Roebuck-Bay-maritime-heritage-office Year-3-pre-arrangement folder at the back of the desk. The rest of the second duffel could wait.
She walked downstairs at six-thirty-five.
The kitchen at six-thirty-five held Yiayia Marigoula at the stove and Phaedon at the table.

The kitchen ran along the north side of the ground floor, with a single window above the sink that looked out onto a small courtyard at the side. The stove was gas. The walls were whitewashed. The walnut table sat at the centre of the floor with six wooden chairs.
The walnut table was the 1925 Phocas-Drosos walnut, original to the house since the Drosos period began.
Phaedon looked up.
Phaedon said: Tia.
Tia said: Phaedon.
Phaedon said: Tuesday five-twenty. The second arrival.
Tia said: yes.
Phaedon said: I came Sunday. First.
Tia said: yes.
Phaedon said: five bedrooms upstairs. One each.
Tia said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula at the stove said: Pothia fish soup. Six-fifty.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Tia sat at the kitchen table next to Phaedon.
She set her hands at the table. She looked at Yiayia Marigoula at the stove, then at Phaedon at her side.
Phaedon said: Aurelia, Athens. Yiayia-Areti, Athens.
Tia said: yes.
Phaedon said: the Drosos-line through my mother. The Trakas-line through my father.
Tia said: yes, Phaedon.
Phaedon said: Yiayia-Marigoula and Yiayia-Areti are cousins of a kind. The Drosos line crosses.
Tia said: yes.
Phaedon said: the line runs.
She held one thought at the back of the chair:
Pothia. Year 1. Two of five.
Dinner ran from six-fifty to seven-forty-five.

Yiayia Marigoula brought the soup at six-fifty in a clay tureen and set it at the table. She brought a board with bread cut in thick slices. She brought a small plate of olives in oil and a smaller plate of cut lemon-wedges. She brought three glasses and a jug of water with ice.
She ladled the soup at Tia’s bowl, then at Phaedon’s, then at her own. She sat at the chair-at-the-head.

The soup was fish-and-tomato with celery and potato. The fish had come off the wharf that morning at six, a small chunk of dorado per bowl. The olive oil and the lemon were Pothia. The bread was Pothia, the loaf the bakery had made at four in the morning.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the Drosos house. Pothia-since-1903.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.

Yiayia Marigoula said: Phocas-the-first built this house in 1903. He had married into Pothia-cooperative-brokerage by then. His daughter Eleni my great-grandmother kept the house. Then her daughter Marioula my grandmother. Then her daughter Marigoula my mother. Then me, since 1985. Fourth-generation.
Tia said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the cohort program took the house in 2024. The Pothia cooperative kept it as the five-lead dorm. Year 1 begins now.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Phaedon.
Phaedon said: Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the Trakas-piano. 1955. First-of-the-twelve. Loukas-Trakas built. Pothia-cooperative-delivery-1955.
Phaedon said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Loukas was your father’s mother’s father. The piano is at the front room.
Phaedon said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Tia.
Tia said: Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the Broome-Theodorakis line. Kalymnian-Australian.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: third and fourth generation. The Pothia return.
Tia said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Eirini Theodorakis. Seventeen. 1908. Pothia-Drosos-cooperative brokerage to Broome.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the brokerage record is at the cooperative archive. Year 1, the search is yours.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the maritime-heritage-office is at the municipal hall. Vouvalis Street. Four blocks up from the port. Stelios will walk you Wednesday next week.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Phaedon said: Stelios.
Yiayia Marigoula said: Stelios Vouvalis. Twenty-six. Junior archivist at the maritime-heritage-office since 2024. Second-floor host-family side of this house. Pre-cohort lodger.
Phaedon said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: he is at Athens this week. Back Sunday.
Phaedon said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: all right.

Tia talked about the five-leg journey, Perth to Pothia, the Singapore overnight, the Athens-Kos hop, the morning ferry. She talked about Carnarvon Street and the family house. She talked about Marisol her sister and Pappous Stathis and Yiayia Marisol Reyes-Coffin and the Sunday-blessing-cards.
She did not talk about her father’s mother’s line. Year 1 private. Pothia conservative.

Phaedon talked about his Sunday arrival and the front-room piano, Pothia-cooperative first-of-the-twelve, the 1955 Loukas-Trakas instrument, the practice pattern he had begun on the Monday. He talked about his Yiayia-Areti at Athens, eighty-six, the Trakas-Alexandria-line through her mother Maria Trakas.
Yiayia Marigoula listened. She nodded at the end of each line.
She said at seven-forty: Tia-mou.
Tia said: Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the line. Pothia-Vathy-Broome. It runs.
Tia said: yes, Yiayia.
Yiayia Marigoula said: the find. Year 1. Slow.
Tia said: yes.
Yiayia Marigoula said: all right.
Dinner closed at seven-forty-five.
Yiayia Marigoula went to her first-floor bedroom at eight.
Tia and Phaedon stayed at the kitchen for the cleanup. The rotation had been set pre-arrival; Tuesday the eighteenth was Phaedon-and-Tia.
Phaedon at the sink said: Tia.
Tia said: Phaedon.
Phaedon said: Tuesday cleanup pair. Two of five.
Tia said: yes.

Phaedon ran the hot water. Tia brought the bowls and the soup-tureen to the sink. The water steamed off. Phaedon washed; Tia dried with the linen towel and set each piece at the wooden drying-rack at the side of the counter. The kitchen window above the sink held the courtyard at evening, the wall of the neighbour’s house, a fig-tree at the corner.
They worked through to eight-twenty.
Phaedon said: the bread board.
Tia handed him the board.
He washed it. He handed it back.
She dried it and set it at the rack.
He said: the soup-pot.
She handed him the pot. He washed it.
He said: the chair-pad covers.
She lifted the four chair-pad covers from the chairs and set them at the basket by the door, the laundry rotation Wednesday morning.
Phaedon said: the table.
He wiped the walnut down with a damp cloth, two passes, the grain running east-to-west.
He set the cloth at the sink and dried his hands at the towel.
Phaedon said: the front-room piano. Twenty minutes. The evening pattern.
Tia said: yes.
They walked to the front room at eight-thirty.

The front room ran along the east side of the ground floor with three tall windows onto the lane and a fourth at the back onto the small courtyard. The 1955 Loukas-Trakas first-of-the-twelve sat at the north wall, an upright in dark walnut with a hinged bench. The piano-shaped its own quiet in the room.
The room held two velvet armchairs at the south side, a bookshelf at the west wall, a low table between the armchairs, and a thin Persian rug.
Phaedon sat at the bench of the 1955 Pothia-cooperative first-of-the-twelve. He set his hands at the keys.
He played the first eight bars of Bach Prelude No. 2 in C minor, BWV 847, slow.
The C-minor opened with the broken-chord pattern, a quarter at a time. The harmonic moved at the bar-line. The room held the lines.

He played a single bar of an Aurelia-1971 arrangement, his mother Aurelia’s childhood-version piano-arrangement of a Trakas family song, the Loukas-Trakas 1933 Alexandrian melody. The single bar opened wide and closed soft. The hinge of the piece in the family.
Tia sat at the velvet armchair.
She listened to the eight bars and the one bar at the front room of the Drosos house at eight-thirty on Tuesday the eighteenth.
She held her hands at her lap.
The west-facing balcony door held the Pothia late-summer evening light.
She thought one sentence at the back of the chair:
The piano.
Phaedon finished at eight-fifty.
He got up from the bench.
He said: Tia.
Tia said: Phaedon.
Phaedon said: good night.
Tia said: good night.
Phaedon walked upstairs at eight-fifty-five.
Tia stayed at the velvet armchair for ten minutes after he went up.

She held the day’s pictures at the back of her head as a single shape: the family house at Carnarvon Street; the Tuesday arrival and the second-of-five place; Phaedon’s Sunday and the front-room piano; her parents and Marisol at Perth airport; the eleven-month Year-1 cohort period that began here, in this front room, on this Tuesday.
She held her hands at her lap.

The bookshelf at the west wall held three rows of Greek-language and English-language books, a small clay pot at the top shelf, and a framed photograph at the second shelf. The photograph was of Phocas-Drosos-the-first at the cooperative-front-desk in 1908 or 1909, taken at the height of the brokerage period.
She got up at nine-ten and walked upstairs to the west bedroom.
She sat at the wooden desk and opened the Moleskine Year-1 archive-notebook. She turned to the first page and wrote:
ē Tuesday 18 August 2026. Pothia. Drosos-house second-floor west bedroom.
ē Second of the five Year-1 cohort arrivals. Phaedon first, 16 Aug. Tia second, 18 Aug. Niko third, 20 Aug (incoming). Lina fourth, 22 Aug (incoming). Athena fifth, 24 Aug (incoming).
ē Yiayia Marigoula, Drosos-house current resident, 76, fourth-generation Drosos, introductory context.
ē Phaedon front-room-piano evening pattern. Bach Prelude C-minor 8 bars. Aurelia-1971 Loukas-Trakas-1933-Alexandrian-song single bar.
ē The walnut kitchen table. 1925 Phocas-Drosos. Original to the Drosos period.

ē Theodorakis-Broome 1908 emigration. Eirini Theodorakis, seventeen, Pothia-Drosos-cooperative brokerage record. Pothia-cooperative archive, Year-1 search. Stelios Vouvalis at the maritime-heritage-office.
ē The line runs.
She closed the Moleskine and set it at the desk.
She walked to the bed. She lay down. She turned off the lamp at ten.
She slept seven hours and forty minutes.
She woke at five-forty on Wednesday the nineteenth of August 2026.
The late-summer pre-dawn light held at the west-facing window. The front-room piano was at the front room. The Year 1 ran.
She held one thought at the back of the chair: Year-1 begins.
The line at the Drosos-cooperative-Pothia-axis. The line at the cooperative-program-Year-1-and-Year-2 Pothia and Year-3-and-Year-4 Broome.
The line runs.
The carrying.
The Year-1-shape held at the back of the chair. The Drosos-house second-floor west-bedroom. The walnut-table at the kitchen. The front-room piano. The five-bedrooms-cohort-pattern.
Phaedon at the front-room-piano at the Bach Prelude C-minor evening-pattern. The 1955-Loukas-Trakas-first-of-the-twelve at the front-room.

The maritime-heritage-office Wednesday-the-twenty-sixth orientation-meeting ahead. Stelios Vouvalis at the junior-archivist-position. Eleni Karavasilis at the senior-archivist-since-1995. The cohort-program-classroom at the municipal-hall.

The cohort-five Year-1 from August 2026 to May 2027. The internship pattern Wed-Thu-Fri at the office. The cooperative-program Year-1 at the four-Greek-cities-cohort-Pothia-cohort. Niko at Darwin-cohort, Athena at Tarpon-cohort, Lina at Sfax-cohort, Phaedon at Alexandria-cohort, Tia at Broome-cohort.
The Pothia-period Year-1-and-Year-2 ahead. The Broome-period Year-3-and-Year-4 future.
The cohort-pact-five-positions at the closing-day Tuesday-the-twenty-fifth-of-June-2030 at five-forty-two-a.m. Broome. Three years and ten months away.
Pothia.
Year 1.
